subject.title: Discrete Mathematics
subject.description: Propositional and first-order logic, sets, relations and functions, partial orders and lattices, groups, counting, recurrences and generating functions, and graph theory, built from first principles with proofs, animated diagrams, Live Labs and every GATE question mapped.

chapters.title: Propositional logic
chapters.summary: Propositions and connectives, truth tables, implication and its relatives, translating English, tautologies and the laws of equivalence, normal forms and functional completeness, and valid arguments, rules of inference and resolution.

chapters.title: First-order logic
chapters.summary: Predicates and quantifiers, translating English with ∀ and ∃, nested quantifiers and their order, negation, interpretations and models, the quantifier laws that do and do not hold, and validity checked by counter-models.

chapters.title: Sets, relations and functions
chapters.summary: Sets, power sets and set identities; relations, their properties, closures and counts; equivalence relations and partitions; functions, composition, inverses and counting maps; countability, infinite sets and the proof techniques (induction above all) used in the rest of the subject.

chapters.title: Partial orders and lattices
chapters.summary: Partial and total orders, Hasse diagrams, extreme elements and bounds, chains, antichains and linear extensions; lattices as orders and as algebras, sublattices, bounded, distributive, complemented and Boolean lattices, and the divisor and subset lattices.

chapters.title: Algebraic structures
chapters.summary: Binary operations and their properties, semigroups and monoids, groups and group tables, abelian and cyclic groups, subgroups, cosets and Lagrange's theorem, modular arithmetic with Fermat and Euler, and a first look at rings and fields.

chapters.title: Combinatorics
chapters.summary: The sum and product rules, permutations, strings and divisors; combinations, the binomial theorem, lattice paths and Catalan numbers; distributions (stars and bars, multisets, partitions, Stirling numbers); inclusion–exclusion, derangements and Euler's totient; the pigeonhole principle; and the sums and series GATE asks for.

chapters.title: Recurrences and generating functions
chapters.summary: Setting up recurrences by looking at the last step, solving them by unrolling, by characteristic roots (distinct, repeated and complex) and particular solutions, reading growth from the dominant root, and generating functions for sequences, recurrences and counting.

chapters.title: Graph theory
chapters.summary: Graphs, degrees and the handshake lemma; isomorphism and complements; paths, connectivity, cut vertices and bridges; trees, forests and spanning trees; Euler and Hamilton; planar graphs and Euler's formula; colouring; and matchings, covers and independent sets.

attrs.title: Further depth: what cannot be decided, and why small domains are not enough

c:
For propositional logic, validity is decidable by truth table. For first-order logic in general it is not:
there is no algorithm that, given any sentence, always halts and says whether it is valid (Church and
Turing, 1936). What does exist is a complete

: every valid sentence has a proof (Gödel's
completeness theorem), so validity is "semi-decidable": search proofs and counter-models in parallel, and if
the sentence is valid the proof search eventually succeeds, but for some invalid sentences (like the
negation of the 1991 sentence) no finite counter-model exists and the counter-model search runs forever.
Some fragments are decidable: the

class of GATE 2018, and sentences with only unary predicates (a
sentence with
unary predicates, if satisfiable, has a model of at most

elements, one per
combination of properties). Finally, if a sentence has an infinite model it has a countable one
(Löwenheim–Skolem), which is why GATE 1991 asks for a countable model.

canonical-table.title: Minterms and maxterms from one table
canonical-table.intro: One truth table gives both canonical forms: true rows become minterms (Σ), false rows become maxterms (Π).

steps.caption: Fill the column of f: p ∧ q is true on TTT and TTF; ¬q ∧ r on TFT and FFT. Four true rows.
Number each row by reading T = 1, F = 0 with p as the most significant bit: TTT is 7, down to FFF = 0.
Each true row gives a minterm, true on that row only. The PDNF is Σ(1, 5, 6, 7).
Each false row gives a maxterm, false on that row only. The PCNF is Π(0, 2, 3, 4): the indices the PDNF left out.
Write each maxterm with plain = 0, negated = 1: row 010 gives p ∨ ¬q ∨ r. The four clauses are the answer to GATE 1995.

completeness-map.title: Post's completeness map
completeness-map.intro: Five properties are preserved by composition. A set of connectives is complete exactly when it can escape each of them.

elements.text: Post's five classes: which connective lies in which
in = the connective lies in that class

steps.caption: Each column is a class closed under composition. A set of connectives is complete only if, in every column, some member of the set says '—' (it escapes).
{∧, ∨, →, ↔}: all four say 'in' under T₁ (they output T on all-T inputs). Trapped: ¬ can never be built, so the set is not complete.
{↔, ¬}: ¬ escapes T₁, but both are 'in' under affine. Everything they build is an XOR-type (linear) function, so ∧ is out of reach.
{¬, ∧}: under every column one of them escapes (¬ escapes T₀, T₁, monotone; ∧ escapes self-dual and affine). Complete.
NAND and NOR are '—' in every column: each escapes all five classes on its own, so each alone is functionally complete.

critical-rows.title: Critical rows decide validity
critical-rows.intro: An argument is valid when the conclusion is true on every row where all premises are true. We mark those critical rows and test two conclusions.

elements.text: Checking an argument only on its critical rows
premises p → q and q → r

steps.caption: Fill the two premise columns. p → q fails only on rows 3 and 4; q → r fails only on rows 2 and 6.
The critical rows are those where every premise is T: rows 1, 5, 7, 8. Only these rows can produce a counterexample.
Conclusion p → r: look at the critical rows only. It is T on all four, so no counterexample exists: the argument is valid (hypothetical syllogism).

set.text: p → r is T on every critical row: valid

steps.caption: Now try the conclusion r → p with the same premises. On critical rows 5 (F T T) and 7 (F F T) it is T → F = F.

set.text: rows 5 and 7: premises T, r → p F

steps.caption: Even one critical row with a false conclusion is a counterexample, so p → q, q → r ∴ r → p is invalid (it is the converse of the valid conclusion). The non-critical rows never matter.

set.text: counterexample p = F, r = T: invalid

custom-operator.title: Rewriting an invented operator
custom-operator.intro: GATE sometimes defines a connective by its four-row table. Read its false row, rewrite it with ¬ and ∨, and the options become easy.

elements.text: An operator given only by its table (GATE 2006)

elements.label: false only at A = F, B = T

steps.caption: Find the false rows of the new operator. There is only one: A = F, B = T.
An operator false on one row is the disjunction that fails there: A ∨ ¬B fails only at A = F, B = T. So A ⊙ B ≡ A ∨ ¬B (which is B → A).
We want A ∧ B = ¬(¬A ∨ ¬B). The option ¬A ⊙ B substitutes ¬A for A: it gives ¬A ∨ ¬B, a NAND.
Negating it gives ¬(¬A ∨ ¬B) = A ∧ B by De Morgan. The answer is ∼(∼A ⊙ B).

fallacy-rows.title: Modus ponens, modus tollens and the two fallacies
fallacy-rows.intro: From p → q you may reason forwards from p or backwards from ¬q. The other two directions are fallacies; the table shows why.

elements.text: Two valid forms and two fallacies on one table

steps.caption: Modus ponens: the critical row (p → q and p both T) is row 1, TT, where q is T. Valid.
Modus tollens: p → q and ¬q are both T only on row 4, FF, where ¬p is T. Valid.
Affirming the consequent: p → q and q are both T on rows 1 and 3. On row 3 (p = F, q = T) the conclusion p is F. Invalid.
Denying the antecedent: p → q and ¬p are both T on rows 3 and 4. On row 3 the conclusion ¬q is F. Invalid.
Both fallacies are defeated by the same row, p = F and q = T: the promise is kept, q holds, and p does not.

set.text: counterexample for both: p = F, q = T

falsify-tree.title: The falsification test
falsify-tree.intro: To test ((a → b) ∧ (b → c)) → (a → c), assume it is false and follow the forced values until they clash or settle.

elements.text: Trying to falsify the hypothetical syllogism

elements.label: so a = T and c = F
so a→b = T and b→c = T
a = T and a → b = T force b = T
b = T and b → c = T force c = T
clash: c = T and c = F

steps.caption: Assume the whole implication is F. An implication is false only as T → F, so the hypothesis must be T and the conclusion F.
The conclusion a → c is F, which forces a = T and c = F. These values are now fixed.
The hypothesis is a true conjunction, so both parts are T: a → b = T and b → c = T.
a is T and a → b is T, so b must be T (otherwise a → b would be T → F).
b is T and b → c is T, so c must be T. But c was already forced to F.
A clash: no row can make the formula false, so it is a tautology. No branching was needed; every value was forced.

implication-promise.title: Implication as a promise
implication-promise.intro: An implication is a promise. It is broken only if the condition happens and the promised result does not.

elements.text: The promise “if you score above 90 (p), you get a prize (q)”

elements.label: T T: scored > 90, got the prize
F T: scored ≤ 90, got a prize

elements.text: p → q is false on one row only

steps.caption: Case T, T: you scored above 90 and got the prize. The promise was kept, so p → q is true.
Case T, F: you scored above 90 and got no prize. This is the one way to break the promise: p → q is false.
Case F, T: you scored 90 or less but got a prize anyway (maybe for something else). The promise said nothing about this case, so it is not broken: true.
Case F, F: you scored 90 or less and got nothing. Again the promise was never tested: true. A false hypothesis makes the implication vacuously true.
So p → q is false exactly when p is true and q is false; that is the same column as ¬p ∨ q.

set.text: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q (false only on T, F)

implication-square.title: Converse, inverse and contrapositive
implication-square.intro: From one implication we can build three others by swapping and negating its two sides. Only one of them says the same thing.

elements.text: The four relatives of an implication

steps.caption: Start from p → q. Swapping the sides gives the converse q → p; negating both sides gives the inverse ¬p → ¬q.
Doing both (swap and negate) gives the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p.
Test the row p = T, q = F. Original: T → F = F. Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p = T → F = F. They fail together.
On the same row the converse is F → T = T and the inverse is F → T = T: they differ from the original, so they are not equivalent to it.
The diagonals pair up: original ≡ contrapositive, and converse ≡ inverse (each is the other's contrapositive).

knights-grid.title: Truth-tellers, liars and a coin
knights-grid.intro: A speaker's statement is true exactly when the speaker is truthful. Tabulate type against coin and keep the worlds where that rule holds.

elements.text: “Head if and only if I am telling the truth” (GATE 2015)
t: the speaker is truthful   h: the coin shows head

steps.caption: List the four possible worlds: the speaker's type times the coin. In each, evaluate the statement h ↔ t.
A truthful speaker's statement must be T and a liar's must be F. Keep a world only if the statement's value matches the type.
Two worlds survive, rows 1 and 3: (truthful, head) and (liar, head). The coin is head in both.
So the result is head, whatever the type; the type itself stays unknown. Algebraically t ↔ (h ↔ t) ≡ h.

set.text: t ↔ (h ↔ t) ≡ h: the coin is head

law-ladder.title: A ladder of laws
law-ladder.intro: Proving an equivalence by laws: one rung per law, arrows out first, then negations in, then tidy up.

elements.text: A rewrite ladder: GATE 2021's consequent becomes its antecedent

steps.caption: Rung 1: remove the outer arrow with A → B ≡ ¬A ∨ B, taking A = P ∧ Q. Always remove arrows first.
Rung 2: implication again. The formula becomes ¬(P ∧ Q) ∨ ¬Q ∨ R.
Rung 3: push the negation inward with De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) becomes ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Now every ¬ sits on a variable.
Rung 4: idempotent: ¬Q ∨ ¬Q ≡ ¬Q. The formula becomes ¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ R.
Rung 5: ¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ R is exactly ¬(P ∧ Q) ∨ R, i.e. (P ∧ Q) → R: the antecedent of S. So S has the shape X → X, a tautology.

set.text: antecedent ≡ consequent, so S ≡ X → X ≡ T

parse-tree.title: Reading a formula as a tree
parse-tree.intro: Precedence turns a string of symbols into a tree. The connective applied last is the root; evaluation runs from the leaves up.

elements.text: The parse tree of ¬p ∨ q ∧ r → p ↔ q
Parse tree of ¬p ∨ q ∧ r → p ↔ q
the root is the main connective

steps.caption: Precedence decides the shape: ¬ binds first, then ∧, then ∨, then →, and ↔ is applied last. So ↔ is the root (the main connective): the formula is a biconditional.
Evaluate at p = F, q = T, r = F. Start at the leaves: write each variable's value.
Lowest operators next: ¬p = T, and q ∧ r = T ∧ F = F.
One level up: ¬p ∨ (q ∧ r) = T ∨ F = T.
The implication has hypothesis T and conclusion p = F: T → F = F, its one false row.
The root compares its two sides: F ↔ T = F, because they disagree. A truth table is this tree evaluated once per row.

set.text: value at p = F, q = T, r = F: F

qlaw-countermodel-search.title: Counter-model search on tiny domains
qlaw-countermodel-search.intro: To refute a law, try every interpretation on a 1-element domain, then a 2-element one. Here the split world P = {0}, Q = {1} appears on size 2.

elements.text: Searching for a counter-model, smallest domain first

steps.caption: Size 1: the domain {0}. There are 4 interpretations (P(0) and Q(0) each T or F). In every one the implication is true: on one element, 'each is P or Q' already means 'all P or all Q'.
Size 2: 16 interpretations of P and Q on {0, 1}. The search tries them in order and the 7th is the first that makes the formula false.
Check the hypothesis in that world: element 0 has P, element 1 has Q, so every element has P or Q. ∀x(P(x) ∨ Q(x)) is T.
Check the conclusion: P fails at 1 and Q fails at 0, so ∀x P(x) and ∀x Q(x) are both F, and so is their disjunction.
T → F: one counter-model, so the formula is not valid. Had sizes 1–3 all passed, we would have learned nothing about validity: only a proof shows that.

qlaw-expansion.title: Quantifiers as long connectives
qlaw-expansion.intro: Over a finite domain, ∀ is an AND and ∃ an OR of one instance per element. The two-way laws are regroupings; the one-way laws are where regrouping fails.

elements.text: ∀ is a long AND, ∃ is a long OR

steps.caption: On the domain {a, b, c}, ∀x(P(x) ∧ Q(x)) is the AND of the P∧Q column: F ∧ T ∧ F.
An AND of ANDs regroups: the same six atoms, sorted into the P column and the Q column. So ∀x(P ∧ Q) ≡ ∀x P ∧ ∀x Q.
Likewise ∃x(P ∨ Q) is the OR of the P∨Q column, and an OR of ORs regroups into ∃x P ∨ ∃x Q.
A mixture does not regroup. ∀x(P ∨ Q) is an AND of ORs: the P∨Q column is all T. But neither the P column nor the Q column is all T.

qlaw-null-flip.title: Null quantification: the flip
qlaw-null-flip.intro: Rewrite the implication as a disjunction, move the quantifier past W, and De Morgan does the flip.

elements.text: Moving ∀ out of a hypothesis flips it to ∃

steps.caption: Remove the arrow: p(x) → W is ¬p(x) ∨ W. The hypothesis is now visibly negated.
W has no free x, so ∀x passes it in a disjunction: ∀x(¬p(x) ∨ W) ≡ (∀x ¬p(x)) ∨ W.
De Morgan for quantifiers: ∀x ¬p(x) is ¬∃x p(x). This is where the ∀ turns into an ∃.
Put the arrow back: ¬∃x p(x) ∨ W is ∃x p(x) → W. One p is enough to force W.
The tempting answer keeps ∀: ∀x p(x) → W (GATE 2020, option C). Test it in the world D = {0, 1}, p = {0}, W = F.
Every rung of the ladder is F there (at x = 0, p(0) → W is T → F), but ∀x p(x) → W is F → F = T. Not equivalent.

qlaw-one-way.title: One-way laws with their counter-models
qlaw-one-way.intro: Each law goes from a strong statement to a weak one. A two-element world with the properties split refutes every converse.

elements.text: Each one-way law, and the world that blocks its converse
domain {0, 1}; the world makes the right side T and the left side F
domain {0, 1}: right side T, left side F

steps.caption: (a) If one predicate holds everywhere, the disjunction does. Converse: 0 has A, 1 has B, so ∀(A ∨ B) is T, but neither ∀A nor ∀B.
(b) A common witness witnesses each part. Converse: ∃A and ∃B are T (0 and 1), but no element has both.
(c) Modus ponens at every element. Converse: ∀A is F, so ∀A → ∀B is vacuously T; but A(0) → B(0) is T → F.
(d) A witness of A is carried to a witness of B. Converse: ∃A → ∃B is T → T, yet A(0) → B(0) fails.
(e) Apply (c) both ways. Converse: ∀A and ∀B are both F, so ∀A ↔ ∀B is T; but A(0) ↔ B(0) is F.
(f) If one A forces all B, each A forces its own B. Converse: ∀(A → B) is T, but ∃A is T and ∀B is F.
(g) Pick any element (domains are non-empty). Converse: ∃A is T at 0, ∀A is F at 1.

qlaw-small-model.title: The small-model property
qlaw-small-model.intro: A model of an ∃∃∃∀∀ sentence without functions, restricted to its three witnesses, is still a model.

elements.text: Keep the witnesses, drop the rest (GATE 2018)
a model with 7 elements: R is < on 0…6

steps.caption: In this 7-element world the sentence is true: for example s = 2, t = 4, u = 6 are witnesses (2 < 4, 4 < 6, 2 ≠ 6, and < is asymmetric).
Send everyone else home: keep only {2, 4, 6}, and keep exactly the pairs of R that lie inside this set.
The ∃ part survives: the witnesses are still present, and R(2, 4), R(4, 6), 2 ≠ 6 are the same atoms as before.
The ∀ part survives: every choice of v, w from {2, 4, 6} was already one of the choices in the big world, and a quantifier-free body without functions only looks at those elements.
So a model with at most 3 elements exists (GATE 2018, option A). With function symbols, or a ∀ before an ∃, a needed element could be outside the kept set.

qlaw-successor-chain.title: Following successors in a finite world
qlaw-successor-chain.intro: A serial, transitive, irreflexive relation on a finite set leads to a contradiction: the successor chain has to loop.

elements.text: Why a serial strict order cannot live in a finite world
4 elements: is R serial, transitive, irreflexive?

steps.caption: Start anywhere, a0. Seriality gives a successor a1 ≠ a0 (irreflexivity forbids a0 → a0).
Keep going: a1 → a2 and a2 → a3. Transitivity already forces a0 → a2, a0 → a3, a1 → a3, so no element can point back to an earlier one without trouble.
a3 needs a successor too. There are only 4 elements and a3 → a3 is forbidden, so it must point back to one already visited, say a1.

set.text: pigeonhole: the chain must revisit an element

steps.caption: Transitivity along the loop: a1 → a3 (from a1 → a2 → a3) and a3 → a1 give a1 → a1. Irreflexivity is violated.
The same happens on every finite domain (an exhaustive search on sizes 1–4 finds no model). In ℕ with <, the chain 0 → 1 → 2 → … never needs to come back.

qlaw-swap-grid.title: The ∃∀ ⇒ ∀∃ grid
qlaw-swap-grid.intro: A relation drawn as a 0/1 grid. ∃y∀x asks for a full column; ∀x∃y asks for a 1 in every row.

elements.text: Rows x, columns y: a full column versus a 1 in every row

steps.caption: This R has a full column, y = 1: every x is related to it. So ∃y∀x R(x, y) is T.
The same column puts a 1 in every row, so every x has a partner: ∀x∃y R(x, y) is T. That is the proof of ∃y∀x ⇒ ∀x∃y: reuse the one witness for every x.
Now a cyclic relation: each row still has exactly one 1, so ∀x∃y R(x, y) stays T, with a different partner for each x.
But no column is full: the partners are y = 1, 2, 0, all different. So ∃y∀x R(x, y) is F, and ∀x∃y ⇒ ∃y∀x fails.

set.text: the witness depends on x: no master key

quant-exactly-one.title: Exactly one
quant-exactly-one.intro: Test any formula for 'exactly one' on three worlds: nobody qualifies, one qualifies, two qualify.

elements.text: “Exactly one” = at least one AND at most one

steps.caption: Three worlds on the domain {1, 2, 3}: nobody has P, exactly one element has P, two elements have P.
Existence, ∃x P(x): false in the empty world, true in the other two. On its own it cannot tell one from two.
Uniqueness, ∀x∀y((P(x) ∧ P(y)) → x = y): true in the empty world (vacuously) and in the one-element world, false with two.
∃x(P(x) ∧ ∀y(P(y) → y = x)) needs both: it is true only in the middle world. That F, T, F pattern is the test for any 'exactly one' option.

quant-negation-ladder.title: The negation ladder
quant-negation-ladder.intro: A negation in front of a block of quantifiers moves inward one quantifier at a time, flipping each one.

steps.caption: Start with the negation in front. It must travel inward past each quantifier.
Passing ∀x turns it into ∃x: 'not for every x' is 'for some x, not'.
Passing ∃y turns it into ∀y: 'not for some y' is 'for every y, not'.
Negate the matrix with Chapter 1's law ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q.
Every quantifier flipped, the ¬ now sits on an atom. The tempting ∃x∀y(P → ¬Q) is wrong: ¬(p → q) is not p → ¬q.

quant-order-grid.title: The order of quantifiers
quant-order-grid.intro: Draw a relation as a grid. 'For every x some y' and 'some y for every x' ask different questions of the same grid.

elements.text: ∀x∃y: a mark in every row.  ∃y∀x: one full column.
rows are x, columns are y; ● marks R(x, y)

steps.caption: The relation is a cycle: a → b, b → c, c → a. Row x has a mark in column y when R(x, y) holds.
∀x∃y R(x, y): for each row, can we find a mark? Row a: column b. Row b: column c. Row c: column a. Yes, every row has one.
∃y∀x R(x, y): is some column full? Each column has exactly one mark, so no single y works for every x.
Now add the pairs (a, a) and (b, a). Column a becomes full: a is a y that works for every x.
A full column puts a mark in every row, so ∃y∀x always implies ∀x∃y. The cycle shows the converse fails.

quant-pairing.title: The pairing rule
quant-pairing.intro: A world with one object outside the subject class (a dog) exposes the wrong pairing of quantifier and connective.

elements.text: “Some cats are black”: why ∃ needs ∧, not →
world: two white cats and a black dog

steps.caption: The world has two cats, neither black, and one black dog. 'Some cats are black' is false here.
Fill the two columns. C ∧ B is T only on a black cat: there is none. C → B is F on each white cat and vacuously T on the dog.
∃x(C ∧ B) is the OR of the C ∧ B column: F. It agrees with the English.
∃x(C → B) is the OR of the C → B column: T, witnessed by the dog, which is not even a cat. It claims something false.
For 'all cats are black' the filter → is right: ∀x(C → B) = F (the white cats are counterexamples) and the dog is ignored.

quant-strip.title: Quantifiers over a domain strip
quant-strip.intro: On a finite domain, ∀ joins the cells with AND and ∃ joins them with OR. One counterexample or one witness decides.

elements.text: ∀ as a big AND, ∃ as a big OR over the domain {1, …, 5}

steps.caption: Fill the strip: P(x) is 'x² > 5'. It is false for 1 and 2 (1 and 4 are not above 5) and true for 3, 4, 5.
∀x P(x) is the AND of all five cells. One F cell is enough to sink an AND.
The very first cell, x = 1, is F: a counterexample. So ∀x P(x) is false; the other cells do not matter.
∃x P(x) is the OR of the same cells. One T cell is enough to make an OR true.
x = 3 is the first T cell: a witness. So ∃x P(x) is true.
The counterexample of ∀ is a witness of ∃¬: x = 1 makes ¬P true. That is De Morgan for quantifiers, ¬∀x P ≡ ∃x ¬P.

resolution-tree.title: A resolution tree
resolution-tree.intro: Resolution proves a conclusion by adding its negation and cancelling complementary literals until the empty clause appears.

elements.text: Resolution refutation: proving r from p ∨ q, p → r, q → r

steps.caption: Write the premises as clauses (p → r is ¬p ∨ r, q → r is ¬q ∨ r) and add the negation of the goal, ¬r. If this set is unsatisfiable, r follows.
Resolve ¬p ∨ r with ¬r on the pair r, ¬r: the resolvent is ¬p.
Resolve ¬q ∨ r with ¬r in the same way: the resolvent is ¬q.
Resolve p ∨ q with ¬p on the pair p, ¬p: the resolvent is q.
Resolve q with ¬q: nothing is left. The empty clause □ is false in every world, so the clause set is unsatisfiable and r follows.

set.text: □ derived: {p ∨ q, p → r, q → r} ⊨ r

rule-chain.title: Contrapositive, then chain
rule-chain.intro: Two implications that do not line up can often be chained after taking a contrapositive.

elements.text: c: known corrupt   e: elected   k: kind

steps.caption: Translate both sentences about one candidate: S1 is c → ¬e and S2 is k → e. The middle letters do not match: one says ¬e, the other e.
Take the contrapositive of S1: c → ¬e is equivalent to e → ¬c. Now e appears as a hypothesis.
S2 ends in e and the rewritten S1 starts with e. Hypothetical syllogism chains them: k → e and e → ¬c give k → ¬c.
k → ¬c is option C: if a person is kind, he is not known to be corrupt. Options A, B and D each have a row with S1 and S2 true and the option false.

sets-bit-ops.title: Set operations on bit strings
sets-bit-ops.intro: Store a subset of an ordered universe as a row of bits. Union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference become OR, AND, AND-NOT and XOR.

elements.text: Sets as bit strings: each operation is one bit rule
U = {1, …, 8}; bit i is 1 iff i is in the set

steps.caption: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6} as 8-bit strings over U = {1, …, 8}: bit i records whether i is in the set.
A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}: OR: 1 if either is 1, position by position, gives 11111100.
A ∩ B = {3, 4}: AND: 1 if both are 1, position by position, gives 00110000.
A − B = {1, 2}: A AND NOT B, position by position, gives 11000000.
A Δ B = {1, 2, 5, 6}: XOR: 1 if they differ, position by position, gives 11001100.

sets-choice-grid.title: Each element chooses
sets-choice-grid.intro: To count pairs of subsets, let every element choose its own membership status. The condition removes some statuses; the rest multiply.

elements.text: Counting pairs (A, B) with A ⊆ B, one element at a time

steps.caption: Each element of S = {1, 2, 3, 4} has four possible statuses: in both sets, in B only, in A only, in neither.
A ⊆ B forbids exactly one status: being in A but not in B. Cross that column out.

set.text: forbidden: in A, not in B

steps.caption: Every element now picks one of 3 statuses, independently of the others, and each choice list is a different pair.
Multiply over the four elements: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81 pairs. An enumeration of all 256 pairs finds exactly 81.
In general 3ⁿ; for |S| = 10 (GATE 2021) that is 3¹⁰ = 59049. Other conditions just change the number of allowed statuses.

sets-membership-table.title: A membership table
sets-membership-table.intro: A membership table is a truth table for set membership. If two expressions have the same final column, they are equal for every choice of sets.

elements.text: A membership table proves A − (B ∩ C) = (A − B) ∪ (A − C)
8 rows: every membership pattern of one element

steps.caption: Each row is one membership pattern of an element (1 = in). Three sets give 2³ = 8 rows, from 111 down to 000.
Column B∩C: 1 only where both B and C are 1 (rows 1 and 5).
Column L = A − (B∩C): 1 where A is 1 and B∩C is 0: rows 2, 3, 4.

set.text: L is A with the triple overlap removed

steps.caption: Columns A−B and A−C: A is 1 and the other set is 0.
Column R is the OR of those two: rows 2, 3, 4 again. Columns L and R agree on all 8 rows, so the sets are equal.

set.text: same column ⇒ same set, for all A, B, C

sets-nesting.title: Element or subset?
sets-nesting.intro: A set is a box; its elements are what lies directly inside. Elements can be boxes too, which is where ∈ and ⊆ part ways.

elements.text: Membership looks one level down; subset unpacks first

steps.caption: The elements of S are the three items directly inside its box: a, the box {b} and the box {a, b}. The b on its own is not one of them.
{b} ∈ S asks: is the box {b} itself lying in S? Yes, it is the middle item. {b} ⊆ S unpacks {b} first: is b in S? No.
{a} ⊆ S unpacks to a, which lies directly in S: true. So a ∈ S and {a} ⊆ S say the same thing.
{a, b} is an element (the third item), but {a, b} ⊆ S fails: unpacking gives a (in S) and b (not in S).
{{b}} ⊆ S unpacks one pair of braces to {b}, which is an element of S: true. Strip one pair of braces for ⊆, none for ∈.

set.text: X ∈ S: listed?   X ⊆ S: unpack, then listed?

sets-powerset-doubling.title: Doubling the power set
sets-powerset-doubling.intro: We add the elements a, b, c one at a time and watch the number of subsets double.

elements.text: Building P({a, b, c}) by doubling

steps.caption: Start with no elements: the only subset is ∅, the empty bit string. One subset.
Add a. Every old subset stays (a out) and gets a twin with a added (a in): ∅ and {a}. Two subsets.

set.text: old ones + old ones with a

steps.caption: Add b. The two old subsets stay and their twins {b}, {a, b} appear. Four subsets: the count doubles.

set.text: old ones + old ones with b

steps.caption: Add c. Four old subsets and four twins with c. Eight subsets, one for each 3-bit string 000 … 111.

set.text: old ones + old ones with c

steps.caption: Each element is an in/out switch, so n elements give 2ⁿ subsets: the bit strings are the subsets.

set.text: each new element doubles the count

sets-venn-regions.title: Comparing expressions by Venn regions
sets-venn-regions.intro: Every expression in A, B, C is a list of some of the 8 Venn regions. Two expressions are equal for all sets exactly when their lists agree.

elements.text: Venn regions: (A − B) − C against (A − C) − (B − C)

steps.caption: Three circles cut the universe into 8 regions, one per membership pattern. Each is named by the sets that contain it; − is outside all.
A − B keeps the part of A outside B: regions AC and A.
Removing C deletes AC. So X = (A − B) − C is the single region A: in A, not in B, not in C.
For Y: A − C = {AB, A} and B − C = {AB, B}.
Removing B − C from A − C deletes AB and leaves the region A. Y has the same region list as X.
Same regions, so X = Y for every choice of A, B, C. Neither is a proper subset of the other.

truth-table-build.title: A truth table, column by column
truth-table-build.intro: The formula (p → q) ∧ (q → r) has three variables. We list all 8 assignments and add one column per sub-formula.

elements.text: Building the table of (p → q) ∧ (q → r), one column at a time
8 rows: p alternates slowest, T before F

steps.caption: Three variables give 2³ = 8 rows. The variable columns are filled first: p is T for the first four rows, q alternates in pairs, r every row.
Column p → q: it is false only where p = T and q = F, which is rows 3 and 4. Every other row keeps the promise.

set.text: p → q fails on rows 3 and 4

steps.caption: Column q → r: false only where q = T and r = F, rows 2 and 6.

set.text: q → r fails on rows 2 and 6

steps.caption: The conjunction is true only where both columns are T: rows 1, 5, 7 and 8 (TTT, FTT, FFT, FFF).
Read the true rows left to right: the values never drop from T to F along p, q, r. The column is the whole meaning of the formula.

set.text: true exactly when p, q, r never go T → F

unless-decoder.title: 'Unless' means 'if not'
unless-decoder.intro: The phrase 'unless Z' turns into the hypothesis 'not Z'. We decode a GATE sentence in three moves.

elements.text: Decoding “if X then Y unless Z”

elements.label: if X then Y  unless Z

steps.caption: Bracket the sentence first. 'Unless Z' qualifies the whole promise 'if X then Y'.
'A unless Z' means 'if not Z, then A'. With A = (X → Y) this is ¬Z → (X → Y).
Exportation moves the outer hypothesis inside: A → (B → C) ≡ (A ∧ B) → C. The result is (X ∧ ¬Z) → Y.
Check with the forbidden situation. The sentence is broken only if X happens, Z does not, and Y fails: X = T, Y = F, Z = F. The formula is false on exactly that row.

set.text: only forbidden row: X = T, Y = F, Z = F

verdict-columns.title: Tautology, contradiction, contingency
verdict-columns.intro: The verdict on a formula is read from its final column: all T, all F, or mixed. Three formulas in p and q, one of each kind.

steps.caption: Column A, q → (p → q): every row is T. A column of all T is a tautology (valid): true whatever p and q mean.
Column B, p ∧ ¬(p ∨ q): every row is F. ¬(p ∨ q) forces p = F, which clashes with the first conjunct. All F is a contradiction (unsatisfiable).
Column C, (p ∨ q) → q: false only on row 2 (p = T, q = F), true elsewhere. A mixed column is a contingency.
Satisfiable means at least one T: A and C are satisfiable, B is not. Falsifiable means at least one F: B and C. Only C is both.

set.text: satisfiable: A, C    falsifiable: B, C

steps.caption: Negating a formula flips its column: ¬A is all F, ¬B is all T, and ¬C is still mixed. Tautology and contradiction swap; contingency stays.
